title: Definition
body_md:
The accessibility relation on $X$ is the binary relation $\preceq$ defined by
\[
x\preceq y
\quad \text{if and only if} \quad
P^n(x,y)>0
\]
for some \(n\in\mathbb N_0\).
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Two states \(x,y\in X\) are said to \emph{communicate} if
\[
x\sim y
\quad \text{if and only if} \quad
x\preceq y
\ \text{and}\
y\preceq x.
\]
The equivalence classes induced by the relation \(\sim\) are called the \emph{communication classes} of the Markov chain.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A discrete-time Markov chain \((X,P)\) is said to be \emph{irreducible} if all states belong to the same communication class. Equivalently,
\[
x\sim y,
\qquad
\forall\, x,y\in X.
\]
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A state \(x\in X\) is said to be \emph{absorbing} if
\[
P(x,x)=1.
\]
Equivalently, once the chain enters the state \(x\), it remains there forever.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A subset \(C\subseteq X\) is said to be \emph{absorbing} if
\[
P(x,C)=1,
\qquad
\forall\,x\in C.
\]
Equivalently, once the chain enters \(C\), it cannot leave \(C\).
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A topological space \((X,\tau)\) is called an \emph{Alexandroff space} if arbitrary intersections of open sets are open.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $(X,\tau)$ be an Alexandroff space. Then, for every
\(x\in X\), there exists a smallest open set containing \(x\),
namely
\[
U_x
=
\bigcap\{U\in\tau:x\in U\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let \((X,\tau)\) be a topological space. The \emph{specialization preorder} on \(X\) is defined by
\[
x\leq_\tau y
\]
if and only if every open set containing \(x\) also contains \(y\).
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $(X,\tau)$ be an Alexandroff space and let
\(x\in X\). Then
\[
\overline{\{x\}}
=
\{y\in X:x\leq_\tau y\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
There is a one-to-one correspondence between Alexandroff topologies on a set \(X\) and preorders on \(X\). More precisely, given a preorder \(\leq\) on \(X\), the associated
Alexandroff topology consists of all downward closed subsets of \(X\).
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
The family
\[
\tau_P=\{U\subseteq X:P^*(U)\subseteq U\}
\]
is an Alexandroff topology on \(X\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify that $\tau_P$ is a topology on $X$. Since $P^*(\varnothing)=\varnothing$, it follows that $\varnothing\in\tau_P$. Moreover, since $P^*(X)\subseteq X$, we also have $X\in\tau_P$. Let $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an arbitrary family of elements of $\tau_P$.
Using the monotonicity of $P^*$, we obtain
\[
P^*\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\right)
=
\bigcup_{i\in I}P^*(U_i).
\]
Since $P^*(U_i)\subseteq U_i$ for every $i\in I$, it follows that
\[
P^*\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\right)
\subseteq
\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i.
\]
Therefore, $\displaystyle{\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau_P}$. Now let $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an arbitrary family of elements of
$\tau_P$. Since $\displaystyle{\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i\subseteq U_j}$ for every $j\in I$, the monotonicity of $P^*$ yields
\[
P^*\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i\right)
\subseteq P^*(U_j)
\]
for every $j\in I$. Hence,
\[
P^*\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i\right)
\subseteq
\bigcap_{i\in I}P^*(U_i).
\]
Since $P^*(U_i)\subseteq U_i$ for every $i\in I$, we conclude that
\[
P^*\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i\right)
\subseteq
\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i.
\]
Thus, $\displaystyle{\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau_P}$. Consequently, $\tau_P$ is a topology closed under arbitrary
intersections, and therefore it is an Alexandroff topology on $X$.
head: environment

label: T1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T1}
Let $(X,P)$ be a discrete-time Markov chain with state space $X$. Then $\preceq$ is a preorder on $X$, and $\tau_P$ coincides with the Alexandroff topology associated with $\preceq$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that the relation $\preceq$ is a preorder on $X$. It is Reflexive, in fact,
for every $x\in X$, $P^0(x,x)=1>0$, where $P^0$ denotes the identity transition matrix. Hence, $x\preceq x$.
It is Transitive.
Suppose that $x\preceq y
\quad \text{and} \quad
y\preceq z$.
Then there exist integers $m,n\in\mathbb N_0$ such that
\[
P^m(x,y)>0
\quad \text{and} \quad
P^n(y,z)>0.
\]
By the Chapman--Kolmogorov equations (cf. Norris~\cite[Section~1.1]{J.R.Norris}),
\[
P^{m+n}(x,z)
=
\sum_{w\in X} P^m(x,w)P^n(w,z).
\]
Since the term corresponding to $w=y$ is strictly positive, we obtain
\[
P^{m+n}(x,z)\ge P^m(x,y)P^n(y,z)>0.
\]
Hence, $x\preceq z$. Therefore, $\preceq$ is transitive, and consequently it is a preorder on $X$. 

\bigskip

Now we prove that $\tau_P$ coincides with the Alexandroff topology associated with $\preceq$. Recall that $U\in\tau_P$ implies
$P^{*}(U)\subseteq U,
$
that is, $P(x,U)>0, \ \ \text{then} \   x\in U$.
We claim that this is equivalent to $U$ being downward closed with respect to $\preceq$. In fact, assume that $U\in\tau_P$, and let $x,y\in X$ such that $x\preceq y
\quad \text{and} \quad
y\in U$. By definition of $\preceq$, there exists $n\in\mathbb N_0$ such that $\displaystyle{P^n(x,y)>0}$. Hence,
\[
P^n(x,U)\ge P^n(x,y)>0.
\]
We prove by induction that
\[
(P^n)^{*}(U)\subseteq U
\qquad \forall n\in\mathbb N_0.
\]
For $n=1$, this is precisely the definition of $\tau_P$. Assume the result holds for some $n\ge1$, and let $\displaystyle{x\in (P^{n+1})^{*}(U)}$, then $\displaystyle{P^{n+1}(x,U)>0}$. Applying the Chapman--Kolmogorov equations,
\[
P^{n+1}(x,U)
=
\sum_{w\in X} P(x,w)P^n(w,U).
\]
Therefore, there exists $w\in X$ such that
\[
P(x,w)>0
\quad \text{and} \quad
P^n(w,U)>0.
\]
Thus,
\[
w\in (P^n)^{*}(U)\subseteq U.
\]
Since $P(x,w)>0$ and $w\in U$, we obtain $\displaystyle{P(x,U)>0}$, which implies
\[
x\in P^{*}(U)\subseteq U.
\]
Hence,
\[
(P^{n+1})^{*}(U)\subseteq U.
\]
By induction,
\[
(P^n)^{*}(U)\subseteq U
\qquad \forall n\in\mathbb N_0.
\]
Since $P^n(x,U)>0$, it follows that
\[
x\in (P^n)^{*}(U)\subseteq U.
\]
Therefore, $U$ is downward closed with respect to $\preceq$. 

\bigskip

Conversely, suppose that $U\subseteq X$ is downward closed with respect to $\preceq$. Let $x\in X$ such that $\displaystyle{P(x,U)>0}$. Then there exists $y\in U$ with $\displaystyle{P(x,y)>0}$. Hence, $x\preceq y$. Since $U$ is downward closed, it follows that $x\in U$. Therefore,
\[
P^{*}(U)\subseteq U,
\]
which proves that $U\in\tau_P$. Consequently, $\tau_P$ coincides with the Alexandroff topology associated with the preorder $\preceq$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $(X,P)$ be a discrete-time Markov chain, and let $\tau_P$ be the Markov accessibility topology on $X$. If the chain is irreducible, then the topological space $(X,\tau_P)$ is connected.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the contrapositive. Suppose that $(X,\tau_P)$ is not connected. Then there exist nonempty disjoint open sets $U,V\in\tau_P$ such that $X=U\cup V$ and
$U\cap V=\varnothing$.
 Let $u\in U$ and $v\in V$. We claim that $u\not\preceq v$. Indeed, suppose by contradiction that $u\preceq v$. Since $v\in V$ and $V$ is open in $\tau_P$, by the Alexandroff characterization of $\tau_P$, the set $V$ is downward closed with respect to $\preceq$. Hence, from $u\preceq v$ and $v\in V$, we obtain $u\in V$. This contradicts $u\in U$ and $U\cap V=\varnothing$. Therefore, $u\not\preceq v$.
Equivalently,
\[
P^n(u,v)=0
\qquad\text{for all } n\in\mathbb N_0.
\]
Thus, $v$ is not accessible from $u$, and so the chain is not irreducible.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Observe that connectedness does not imply irreducibility. Indeed, consider the two-state Markov chain
\[
1\to 2,
\]
whose Markov primal topology is
\[
\tau_P=\{\varnothing,\{1\},\{1,2\}\}.
\]
This topology is connected, although the chain is not irreducible, since state $1$ is not accessible from state $2$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The equivalence between $(1)$ and $(2)$ follows directly from the definition of irreducibility. We now prove that $(2)$ implies $(3)$. Assume that
\[
x\preceq y
\qquad \text{for all } x,y\in X.
\]
Let \(U\in\tau_P\) be nonempty. Choose \(y\in U\). Since \(x\preceq y\) for every \(x\in X\), and since \(U\) is open, it follows from the Alexandroff characterization of \(\tau_P\) that \(U\) is downward closed with respect to \(\preceq\). Hence,
\[
x\in U
\qquad \text{for every } x\in X.
\]
Therefore, $U=X$. Thus the only open subsets of \(X\) are \(\varnothing\) and \(X\), and so $\tau_P=\{\varnothing,X\}$. It remains to prove that $(3)$ implies $(2)$. Assume that
\[
\tau_P=\{\varnothing,X\}.
\]
Suppose, by contradiction, that there exist \(x,y\in X\) such that
\[
x\not\preceq y.
\]
Consider the set
\[
U_y:=\{z\in X:z\preceq y\}.
\]
By reflexivity of \(\preceq\), we have \(y\in U_y\), so \(U_y\neq\varnothing\). Moreover, since \(x\not\preceq y\), we have \(x\notin U_y\), and hence \(U_y\neq X\). We claim that \(U_y\in\tau_P\). Indeed, let \(a,b\in X\) with
\[
a\preceq b
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
b\in U_y.
\]
Since \(b\in U_y\), we have \(b\preceq y\). By transitivity of \(\preceq\),
\[
a\preceq y.
\]
Thus \(a\in U_y\). Therefore \(U_y\) is downward closed with respect to \(\preceq\), and by the Alexandroff characterization of \(\tau_P\), Theorem \ref{T1}, it follows that $U_y\in\tau_P$. Hence \(U_y\) is a nonempty proper open subset of \(X\) which is a contradiction.
Therefore,
\[
x\preceq y
\qquad \text{for all } x,y\in X.
\]
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
A subset $C\subseteq X$ is closed in $(X,\tau_P)$ if and only if
\[
P(x,C)=1
\qquad \text{for all } x\in C.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $C$ is closed in $(X,\tau_P)$. Then its complement $U:=X\setminus C$ is open in $\tau_P$. Hence, by the definition of the Markov primal topology, $\displaystyle{P^{*}(U)\subseteq U}$. Let $x\in C$. Since $x\notin U$, the inclusion above implies that $x\notin P^{*}(U)$. Therefore, $\displaystyle{P(x,U)=0}$. Since $U=X\setminus C$, we have $\displaystyle{P(x,X\setminus C)=0}$. Consequently, $\displaystyle{P(x,C)=1}$. Thus,
\[
P(x,C)=1
\qquad \text{for all } x\in C.
\]
Conversely, assume that
\[
P(x,C)=1
\qquad \text{for all } x\in C.
\]
We prove that $C$ is closed by showing that its complement $\displaystyle{U:=X\setminus C}$ is open. Let $x\in P^{*}(U)$. Then $\displaystyle{P(x,U)>0}$. We claim that $x\in U$. Indeed, if $x\in C$, then by hypothesis
\[
P(x,C)=1,
\]
and therefore
\[
P(x,U)=P(x,X\setminus C)=0,
\]
which contradicts $P(x,U)>0$. Hence $x\notin C$, and so $x\in U$. Therefore,
\[
P^{*}(U)\subseteq U,
\]
which means that $U\in\tau_P$. Hence $X\setminus C$ is open, and consequently $C$ is closed in $(X,\tau_P)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The previous theorem shows that the closed sets of the Markov accessibility topology are precisely the absorbing subsets of the chain. In particular, singleton closed sets correspond to absorbing states, while more general closed sets correspond to closed communicating structures in the classical theory of Markov chains.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: For $x\in X$, the singleton set $\{x\}$ is closed in $(X,\tau_P)$ if and only if $x$ is an absorbing state.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the previous theorem, a subset $C\subseteq X$ is closed in $(X,\tau_P)$ if and only if
\[
P(y,C)=1
\qquad \text{for all } y\in C.
\]
Taking $C=\{x\}$, we obtain that $\{x\}$ is closed if and only if
\[
P(x,\{x\})=1.
\]
Since
\[
P(x,\{x\})=P(x,x),
\]
it follows that
\[
P(x,x)=1,
\]
which is precisely the definition of an absorbing state.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: If $(X,P)$ is an irreducible discrete-time Markov chain, then the only closed subsets of $(X,\tau_P)$ are $\varnothing$ and $X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem 3, if $(X,P)$ is irreducible, then
\[
\tau_P=\{\varnothing,X\},
\]
that is, $\tau_P$ is the trivial topology on $X$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $X=\{1,2,3\}$ and consider the discrete-time Markov chain with transition matrix
\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1\\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This chain corresponds to the deterministic cycle
\[
1\to2\to3\to1.
\]
For any $x,y\in X$, there exists $n\ge0$ such that
\[
P^n(x,y)>0.
\]
Hence, the chain is irreducible. By Theorem 3, the Markov accessibility topology $\tau_P$ consists only of the trivial subsets. Since every state is accessible from every other state, it follows that any nonempty downward closed subset must contain all elements of $X$. Therefore,
\[
\tau_P=\{\varnothing,X\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $X=\{1,2\}$ and consider the Markov chain with transition matrix
\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1\\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
In this case,
\[
1\to2,
\qquad
2\to2.
\]
The accessibility relation satisfies
\[
1\preceq1,
\qquad
1\preceq2,
\qquad
2\preceq2,
\]
but
\[
2\not\preceq1.
\]
Hence, the chain is not irreducible. The downward closed subsets of $X$ are
\[
\varnothing,
\qquad
\{1\},
\qquad
\{1,2\}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\tau_P=\{\varnothing,\{1\},X\}.
\]
This topology is connected, since there do not exist two nonempty disjoint open subsets whose union is $X$. However, the chain is reducible. The closed subsets are
\[
\varnothing,
\qquad
\{2\},
\qquad
X.
\]
Indeed,
\[
P(2,\{2\})=1,
\]
so the state $2$ is absorbing.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $(X,P)$ be a discrete-time Markov chain, and let $\preceq$ be the accessibility preorder associated with the chain. For each $x\in X$, define
\[
P_P(x):=\{y\in X:y\preceq x\}.
\]
We refer to $P_P(x)$ as the \emph{minimal open set associated with} $x$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $x\in X$. We prove the three assertions separately. First, we show that $P_P(x)$ is open. By definition,
\[
P_P(x)=\{y\in X:y\preceq x\}.
\]
Let $z\in P_P(x)$ and suppose that $y\preceq z$. Since $z\in P_P(x)$, we have $z\preceq x $.
By transitivity of the accessibility preorder, $y\preceq x$. Hence, $y\in P_P(x)$. Therefore, $P_P(x)$ is downward closed with respect to $\preceq$. By the Alexandroff characterization of $\tau_P$, it follows that
\[
P_P(x)\in\tau_P.
\]
Second, since $\preceq$ is reflexive, we have $x\preceq x$. Thus,
\[
x\in P_P(x).
\]
Finally, let $U\in\tau_P$ be such that $x\in U$. Since $U$ is open, it is downward closed with respect to $\preceq$. If $y\in P_P(x)$, then
\[
y\preceq x.
\]
By the facts that $x\in U$ and $U$ is downward closed, we obtain $y\in U$. Hence,
\[
P_P(x)\subseteq U.
\]
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
The family $\mathcal{B}:=\{P_P(x):x\in X\}$ forms a basis for Markov accessibility topology $\tau_P$. In particular, for every $U\in\tau_P$,
\[
U=\bigcup_{x\in U} P_P(x).
\]
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
For $x,y\in X$, $\displaystyle{x\preceq y
 \ \text{if and only if} \ 
P_P(x)\subseteq P_P(y)}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Assume that $x\preceq y$. Let $z\in P_P(x)$. Then $z\preceq x$. By transitivity of the accessibility preorder, $z\preceq y$. Hence, $z\in P_P(y)$. Therefore, $P_P(x)\subseteq P_P(y)$. Conversely, suppose that $P_P(x)\subseteq P_P(y)$. Since $\preceq$ is reflexive, $x\preceq x$, and therefore $x\in P_P(x)$. By the inclusion hypothesis, $x\in P_P(y)$. Hence, $x\preceq y$. This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
For $x,y\in X$, $P_P(x)=P_P(y)
\ \text{if and only if} \ \ 
x\sim y$. Hence, the minimal open sets are constant on communication classes.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first that $P_P(x)=P_P(y)$. By the previous proposition, $P_P(x)\subseteq P_P(y) \ \  \text{if and only if}\  \  x\preceq y$, and similarly, $P_P(y)\subseteq P_P(x)
 \ \ \text{if and only if} \ \  y\preceq x$. Since the two sets are equal, both inclusions hold. Therefore, $x\preceq y
 \ \text{and} \ 
y\preceq x$, which means that $x\sim y$. Conversely, suppose that $x\sim y$. Then $x\preceq y
 \ \  \text{and} \  \ 
y\preceq x$. Again by the previous proposition, $P_P(x)\subseteq P_P(y) \ \ \text{and} \ \ 
P_P(y)\subseteq P_P(x)$. Hence, $P_P(x)=P_P(y)$.
head: environment

label: T:hitting
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that \(U\in\tau_P\). We prove that $\displaystyle{ \mathbb P_y(\tau_U<\infty)=0
 \ \text{for every } y\in X\setminus U}$. Let \(y\in X\setminus U\). If, by contradiction,
$ \displaystyle{
\mathbb P_y(\tau_U<\infty)>0
}$,
then there exists \(n\in\mathbb N_0\) such that
\[
\mathbb P_y(X_n\in U)>0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
P^n(y,U)>0.
\]
Hence, there exists \(x\in U\) such that
\[
P^n(y,x)>0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
y\preceq x.
\]
Since \(U\in\tau_P\), by the Alexandroff characterization of the Markov accessibility topology, Theorem \ref{T1},  \(U\) is downward closed with respect to \(\preceq\). Thus, from \(y\preceq x\) and \(x\in U\), we obtain
\[
y\in U,
\]
which contradicts \(y\in X\setminus U\). Hence,
\[
\mathbb P_y(\tau_U<\infty)=0.
\]
Conversely, assume that
\[
\mathbb P_y(\tau_U<\infty)=0
 \  \text{for every } y\in X\setminus U.
\]
Let \(y\in X\) and \(x\in U\) be such that
\[
y\preceq x.
\]
Then there exists \(n\in\mathbb N_0\) such that
\[
P^n(y,x)>0.
\]
Since \(x\in U\), it follows that
\[
P^n(y,U)>0.
\]
Thus,
\[
\mathbb P_y(\tau_U<\infty)>0.
\]
By the hypothesis, this is impossible if \(y\in X\setminus U\). Therefore, $y\in U$. Hence, \(U\) is downward closed with respect to \(\preceq\). By the Alexandroff characterization of \(\tau_P\), we conclude that $\displaystyle{U\in\tau_P}$.
head: environment

label: T:pathwise
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T:pathwise}
For a subset $U\subseteq X$, define the exit time from $U$ by
\[
\sigma_U:=\inf\{n\in\mathbb N_0:X_n\notin U\},
\]
Then the following statements are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item $U\in\tau_P$;

    \item for every initial distribution $\mu$ on $X$, the process
    \[
    \bigl(\mathbf 1_U(X_n)\bigr)_{n\geq 0}
    \]
    is $\mathbb P_\mu$-almost surely non-increasing;

    \item for every initial distribution $\mu$ on $X$,
    \[
    \mathbb P_\mu
    \bigl(
    \sigma_U<\infty,\,
    \tau_U\circ\theta_{\sigma_U}<\infty
    \bigr)
    =0.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
The random variable
\[
\tau_U\circ\theta_{\sigma_U}
\]
represents the first return time to \(U\) after the exit time \(\sigma_U\). In other words, once the chain exits the set \(U\), it cannot return to \(U\) with positive probability.
head: environment
name: Pathwise characterization of open sets

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $U\in\tau_P$. By definition of the Markov primal topology,
\[
P^{*}(U)\subseteq U.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
P(x,U)=0,
\qquad
\forall\,x\in X\setminus U.
\]
Let $\mu$ be any initial distribution. For each $n\geq0$, consider the event
\[
A_n:=\{X_n\notin U,\ X_{n+1}\in U\}.
\]
We claim that
\[
\mathbb P_\mu(A_n)=0.
\]
Indeed,
\[
\mathbb P_\mu(A_n)
=
\mathbb E_\mu
\!\left[
\mathbf 1_{\{X_n\notin U\}}
\mathbf 1_{\{X_{n+1}\in U\}}
\right].
\]
Using the Markov property,
\[
\mathbb P_\mu(A_n)
=
\mathbb E_\mu
\!\left[
\mathbf 1_{\{X_n\notin U\}}
P(X_n,U)
\right].
\]
Since $P(x,U)=0$ for every $x\notin U$, the integrand vanishes identically. Hence
\[
\mathbb P_\mu(A_n)=0
\qquad
\forall\,n\geq0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb P_\mu
\!\left(
\bigcup_{n\ge0}A_n
\right)
=
0.
\]
In other words, with probability one the trajectory can never make a transition from
$X\setminus U$ into $U$. Consequently,
$\displaystyle{
\bigl(\mathbf 1_U(X_n)\bigr)_{n\ge0}
}$ is $\mathbb P_\mu$-almost surely non-increasing. Now, we assume that for every initial distribution $\mu$,
$ \displaystyle{
\bigl(\mathbf 1_U(X_n)\bigr)_{n\ge0}
}$ is $\mathbb P_\mu$-almost surely non-increasing. We are going to show that $U\in\tau_P$. It suffices to prove that
\[
P(x,U)=0,
\qquad
\forall\,x\in X\setminus U.
\]
Fix $x\in X\setminus U$ and choose the initial distribution
$\displaystyle{
\mu=\delta_x.
}$
Then
\[
\mathbf 1_U(X_0)=0
\qquad
\mathbb P_{\delta_x}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Since the indicator process is almost surely non-increasing,
\[
\mathbf 1_U(X_1)=0
\qquad
\mathbb P_{\delta_x}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb P_{\delta_x}(X_1\in U)=0,
\]
that is, $\displaystyle{P(x,U)=0}$. Since $x\in X\setminus U$ was arbitrary, $\displaystyle{P^{*}(U)\subseteq U}$. Therefore, $\displaystyle{U\in\tau_P}$. Now, we suppose that for every initial distribution $\mu$,
$ \displaystyle{
\bigl(\mathbf 1_U(X_n)\bigr)_{n\ge0}
}$ is $\mathbb P_\mu$-almost surely non-increasing.
Fix an initial distribution $\mu$.
On the event $\{\sigma_U<\infty\}$, the chain exits $U$ at time $\sigma_U$, so $\displaystyle{X_{\sigma_U}\notin U}$. Since the indicator process is non-increasing, once it reaches the value $0$ it can never return to the value $1$. Therefore the shifted trajectory $\displaystyle{(X_{\sigma_U+n})_{n\ge0}}$ never hits $U$. Equivalently,
\[
\tau_U\circ\theta_{\sigma_U}
=
\infty
 \  \ 
\text{on } \ \ \{\sigma_U<\infty\},
\]
almost surely. Hence
\[
\mathbb P_\mu
\bigl(
\sigma_U<\infty,
\,
\tau_U\circ\theta_{\sigma_U}<\infty
\bigr)
=
0.
\]
Finally, assume that for every initial distribution $\mu$,
\[
\mathbb P_\mu
\bigl(
\sigma_U<\infty,
\,
\tau_U\circ\theta_{\sigma_U}<\infty
\bigr)
=
0.
\]
Fix an initial distribution $\mu$. We show that
\[
\bigl(\mathbf 1_U(X_n)\bigr)_{n\ge0}
\]
is $\mathbb P_\mu$-almost surely non-increasing. Suppose, to the contrary, that the indicator process is not non-increasing on some trajectory. Then there exist integers $m<n$ such that
\[
X_m\notin U,
\qquad
X_n\in U.
\]
Let $\sigma_U$ be the first exit time from $U$. Then $\displaystyle{\sigma_U<\infty}$, and there exists a later time at which the chain returns to $U$. Consequently,
\[
\tau_U\circ\theta_{\sigma_U}<\infty.
\]
Thus the trajectory belongs to the event
\[
\{\sigma_U<\infty,
\,
\tau_U\circ\theta_{\sigma_U}<\infty\},
\]
which has probability zero by assumption. Therefore the set of trajectories for which
$\displaystyle{
\bigl(\mathbf 1_U(X_n)\bigr)_{n\ge0}
}$
fails to be non-increasing has probability zero. Hence the process is
$\mathbb P_\mu$-almost surely non-increasing.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For \(x\in X\), let $\displaystyle{\tau_x:=\inf\{n\in\mathbb N_0:X_n=x\}}$ denote the first hitting time of the state \(x\). Then,
\[
P_x(x)
=
\{y\in X:\mathbb P_y(\tau_x<\infty)>0\}.
\]
Precisely, the minimal open neighborhood of \(x\) is precisely the set of states from which \(x\) can be hit with positive probability.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition of the minimal open neighborhood,
\[
P_P(x)=\{y\in X:y\preceq x\}.
\]
Thus, \(y\in P_P(x)\) if and only if $y\preceq x$. By definition of the accessibility relation, this is equivalent to the existence of some
\(n\in\mathbb N_0\) such that $\displaystyle{P^n(y,x)>0}$. On the other hand,
\[
\mathbb P_y(\tau_x<\infty)>0
\]
if and only if the chain, starting from \(y\), reaches \(x\) at some finite time with positive probability. This is equivalent to saying that there exists \(n\in\mathbb N_0\) such that
\[
\mathbb P_y(X_n=x)>0.
\]
Since
\[
\mathbb P_y(X_n=x)=P^n(y,x),
\]
we obtain that
\[
\mathbb P_y(\tau_x<\infty)>0
\]
holds if and only if there exists \(n\in\mathbb N_0\) such that $\displaystyle{P^n(y,x)>0}$. Therefore, $y\in P_P(x)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
For each state \(x\in X\), the set
\[
[x]
=
\{y\in X : y\sim x\}
\]
is called the \emph{communication class} of \(x\). The quotient set
\[
X/{\sim}
=
\{[x] : x\in X\}
\]
is called the \emph{communication quotient space}.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: The relation \(\preceq_q\) on \(X/{\sim}\) is well defined.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \([x],[y]\in X/{\sim}\). We need to show that the definition
\[
[x]\preceq_q [y]
\quad \text{if and only if} \quad
x\preceq y
\]
does not depend on the choice of representatives. Suppose that
\[
[x]=[x']
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
[y]=[y'].
\]
This means that
\[
x\sim x'
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
y\sim y'.
\]
Therefore,
\[
x'\preceq x
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
y\preceq y'.
\]
Now assume that $x\preceq y$. Using the transitivity of the accessibility preorder, we obtain
\[
x'\preceq x\preceq y\preceq y'.
\]
Hence,
\[
x'\preceq y'.
\]
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The relation \(\preceq_q\) is a partial order on the communication quotient \(X/{\sim}\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove that \(\preceq_q\) is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. First, let \([x]\in X/{\sim}\). Since the accessibility preorder \(\preceq\) is reflexive, we have $x\preceq x$. Therefore, by definition of \(\preceq_q\),
\[
[x]\preceq_q [x].
\]
Thus, \(\preceq_q\) is reflexive. Now suppose that $[x]\preceq_q [y]$ and $[y]\preceq_q [x]$. By definition of \(\preceq_q\), this means that $x\preceq y$ and
$y\preceq x$. Hence,
\[
x\sim y.
\]
Therefore,
\[
[x]=[y].
\]
Thus, \(\preceq_q\) is antisymmetric. Finally, suppose that $[x]\preceq_q [y]$ and $[y]\preceq_q [z]$, which means that $x\preceq y$ and $y\preceq z$. Since \(\preceq\) is transitive, it follows that $x\preceq z$. Therefore,
\[
[x]\preceq_q [z].
\]
Thus, \(\preceq_q\) is transitive.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: The Alexandroff topology on \(X/{\sim}\) induced by the partial order \(\preceq_q\) is \(T_0\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It is a classical fact that an Alexandroff topology is \(T_0\) if and only if its associated preorder is antisymmetric. Since \(\preceq_q\) is a partial order on \(X/{\sim}\), it is antisymmetric. Therefore, the Alexandroff topology induced by \(\preceq_q\) is \(T_0\).
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A discrete-time Markov chain \((X,P)\) is said to be \emph{lumpable} with respect to the communication partition if
\[
P(x,[z])=P(y,[z]),
\qquad
\forall\,x,y\in[w],\quad \forall\,[w],[z]\in X/{\sim},
\]
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let \((X_n)_{n\geq0}\) be a discrete-time Markov chain with transition matrix \(P\), and suppose that the chain is lumpable with respect to the partition of \(X\) into communication classes. Then the following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item The process \((Y_n)_{n\geq0}\) is a discrete-time Markov chain on \(X/{\sim}\).

    \item Its transition matrix is given by
    \[
    \overline{P}([x],[y])
    =
    P(x,[y]),
    \]

    where
    \[
    P(x,[y])
    =
    \sum_{z\in[y]}P(x,z).
    \]
   
    \item The accessibility relation of the quotient chain coincides with the partial order \(\preceq_q\).

    \item the Markov accessibility topology associated with the quotient transition matrix \(\overline P\) coincides with the Alexandroff topology induced by the partial order \(\preceq_q\).
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, the lumpability condition ensures that the quantity
\[
\overline P([x],[y]) := P(x,[y])
\]
is well defined. Indeed, if \(x'\in[x]\), then by lumpability,
\[
P(x,[y])=P(x',[y]).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\overline P([x],[y])\geq 0
\]
and
\[
\sum_{[y]\in X/{\sim}}\overline P([x],[y])
=
\sum_{[y]\in X/{\sim}}P(x,[y])
=
\sum_{z\in X}P(x,z)
=
1.
\]
Hence \(\overline P\) is a stochastic matrix on \(X/{\sim}\). Now let
\[
Y_n=q(X_n)=[X_n].
\]
For communication classes \([x]\) and \([y]\), we have
\[
\mathbb P(Y_{n+1}=[y]\mid Y_n=[x])
=
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in[y]\mid X_n\in[x]).
\]
By the lumpability condition, the total probability of moving from the class \([x]\) to the class \([y]\) does not depend on the representative \(x\in[x]\). Therefore,
\[
\mathbb P(Y_{n+1}=[y]\mid Y_n=[x])
=
\overline P([x],[y]).
\]
More generally, conditioning on the whole past of \(Y\), the same argument gives
\[
\mathbb P(Y_{n+1}=[y]\mid Y_n,[Y_{n-1}],\ldots,Y_0)
=
\overline P(Y_n,[y]).
\]
Thus \((Y_n)_{n\geq0}\) is a discrete-time Markov chain on \(X/{\sim}\) with transition matrix \(\overline P\). It remains to identify its accessibility relation. Suppose first that
\[
[x]\preceq_q [y].
\]
By definition, this means that $\displaystyle{x\preceq y}$. Hence there exists \(n\in\mathbb N_0\) such that
\[
P^n(x,y)>0.
\]
Therefore, starting from the class \([x]\), the projected chain can reach the class \([y]\) in \(n\) steps with positive probability. Thus \([y]\) is accessible from \([x]\) for the quotient chain. Conversely, suppose that \([y]\) is accessible from \([x]\) for the quotient chain. Then there exists \(n\in\mathbb N_0\) such that
\[
\overline P^{\,n}([x],[y])>0.
\]
This means that the projected chain can move from \([x]\) to \([y]\) with positive probability in \(n\) steps. Hence there exist representatives along such a path in the original chain, and consequently some state in \([y]\) is accessible from some state in \([x]\). Since all states inside a communication class communicate with each other, it follows that $\displaystyle{x\preceq y}$. Therefore,
\[
[x]\preceq_q [y].
\]
Thus the accessibility relation of the quotient chain coincides with the partial order \(\preceq_q\). Finally, by Theorem~\ref{T1}, the Markov accessibility topology associated with the quotient transition matrix \(\overline P\) is the Alexandroff topology generated by the accessibility relation of the quotient chain. Since this accessibility relation is precisely \(\preceq_q\), the Markov accessibility topology generated by \(\overline P\) coincides with the canonical \(T_0\)-Alexandroff topology on \(X/{\sim}\) induced by the partial order \(\preceq_q\).
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the discrete-time Markov chain with state space
\[
X=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\},
\]
whose transition matrix is
\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac12 & \frac12 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
\frac13 & \frac13 & \frac13 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & \frac12 & \frac12 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0 & \frac12 & \frac12 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0 & \frac14 & \frac14 & \frac12 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac12 & \frac12\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac12 & \frac12
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The communication classes of the chain are
\[
[1]=\{1,2\},\qquad
[3]=\{3\},\qquad
[4]=\{4,5\},\qquad
[6]=\{6,7\}.
\]
The accessibility relation induces the partial order
\[
[1]\preceq_q[3]\preceq_q[4]\preceq_q[6].
\]
Consequently, the communication quotient is the totally ordered set
\[
X/{\sim}
=
\bigl\{
[1],[3],[4],[6]
\bigr\},
\]
whose Hasse diagram is

\[
[1]
\longrightarrow
[3]
\longrightarrow
[4]
\longrightarrow
[6].
\]
The minimal open neighborhoods are given by
\[
P_P(1)=P_P(2)=\{1,2\},
\]

\[
P_P(3)=\{1,2,3\},
\]

\[
P_P(4)=P_P(5)=\{1,2,3,4,5\},
\]

and

\[
P_P(6)=P_P(7)=X.
\]

Hence, the Markov accessibility topology is

\[
\tau_P=
\{
\varnothing,
\{1,2\},
\{1,2,3\},
\{1,2,3,4,5\},
X
\}.
\]

Its closed sets are

\[
\varnothing,
\{6,7\},
\{4,5,6,7\},
\{3,4,5,6,7\},
X,
\]

which coincide with the absorbing subsets of the chain. Moreover, the partition into communication classes is lumpable. Therefore, the projected process $\displaystyle{Y_n=[X_n]}$ is itself a Markov chain on the quotient space \(X/{\sim}\), whose transition matrix is

\[
\overline P=
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac23 & \frac13 & 0 & 0\\
0 & \frac12 & \frac12 & 0\\
0 & 0 & \frac12 & \frac12\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
